title: Karl Marx

scenes.title: Karl Marx, 1818–1883
scenes.narration: Karl Marx was a philosopher, economist, journalist and revolutionary who spent most of his adult life as a stateless exile in London. His analysis of capitalism, much of it researched in the reading room of the British Museum, inspired both the social democratic parties of Europe and the communist states of the twentieth century. Few thinkers have been so influential or so fiercely argued over, and this course tries to separate the man and his ideas from what was later done in his name.

scenes.title: From Trier to London, 1818–1849
scenes.narration: Marx was born in Trier, in the Prussian Rhineland, on 5 May 1818, the son of a lawyer of Jewish descent who had become a Protestant. He studied in Bonn and Berlin, where he joined the radical young followers of the philosopher Hegel, and he edited a liberal newspaper in Cologne until the Prussian government banned it in 1843. He then moved to Paris, was expelled to Brussels in 1845, returned to Cologne in the revolution of 1848, and after its defeat settled in London in 1849.

scenes.title: Friedrich Engels
scenes.narration: In Paris in 1844 Marx began a lifelong partnership with Friedrich Engels, the son of a German textile manufacturer whose family firm had a share in a mill in Manchester. Engels's book on the condition of the English working class appeared in 1845, and that summer the two men travelled together to Manchester. For decades Engels's income from the family business kept the Marx household afloat in London, through years of poverty in which only three of Marx's seven children lived to adulthood.

In February 1848 a pamphlet written by Marx and Engels for a small group called the Communist League was printed in London: the Manifesto of the Communist Party. That same month revolution broke out in Paris, and within weeks in Vienna, Berlin, Milan and Budapest, though the Manifesto itself played little part in any of them. By the end of 1849 the old order had been restored almost everywhere.

scenes.title: History and class struggle
scenes.narration: At the centre of Marx's thought is the claim that the way a society produces its material needs shapes its laws, politics and ideas, an approach later called historical materialism. The Manifesto declared that the history of all society so far is the history of class struggles, and that capitalism, by creating an industrial working class, was producing its own gravediggers. In a preface of 1859 Marx put the principle in a single sentence.

visual.text: It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but, on the contrary, their social existence determines their consciousness.
visual.who: Karl Marx, preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, translated by N. I. Stone

scenes.title: Capital, 1867
scenes.narration: The first volume of Capital appeared in Hamburg in 1867. Building on Adam Smith and David Ricardo, Marx argued that labour creates value, and that profit comes from surplus value, the part of what workers produce for which they are not paid. Competition, he believed, forces capitalists to accumulate and mechanise, concentrating capital in fewer hands and producing recurring crises.

scenes.title: Wages and output in industrial Britain
scenes.narration: Engels's book of 1845 described a Britain in which output was growing fast while workers' living standards barely rose. The economic historian Robert Allen has called this Engels' pause: by his estimates, between 1780 and 1840 output per worker rose by about 46 per cent but real wages by only about 12, and from 1840 to 1900 wages rose faster than output. Other economic historians, among them Nicholas Crafts, find that the gap before 1840 was smaller. Whether capitalism must keep workers poor became one of the great arguments over Marx's legacy.

scenes.title: Critics and defenders
scenes.narration: From the 1870s most economists abandoned the labour theory of value for theories built on marginal utility, and critics argued that Marx's predictions of capitalist collapse were not borne out. Leszek Kołakowski, a Polish philosopher who broke with communism, argued that Stalinism was one possible reading of Marx's ideas rather than simply a betrayal of them. Eric Hobsbawm, a lifelong Marxist historian, held that Marx's analysis of how capitalism works, and of its crises, remained relevant.

scenes.title: The International, and the last years, 1864–1894
scenes.narration: In 1864 Marx helped found the International Working Men's Association in London, and in 1871 his defence of the Paris Commune made him notorious. His wife Jenny died in 1881, and Marx died in London on 14 March 1883; at his graveside in Highgate Cemetery, Engels compared his friend's discoveries to Darwin's. Engels then edited the second and third volumes of Capital, which appeared in 1885 and 1894.

scenes.title: Parties and revolutions, 1875–1949
scenes.narration: Marx's ideas spread first through mass parties such as Germany's Social Democrats, the largest party in the Reichstag by 1912, many of whose leaders came to seek socialism through elections rather than revolution. In Russia, Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in 1917 in Marx's name. After the Second World War communist parties came to rule most of eastern Europe and, from 1949, China.

scenes.title: In his name
scenes.narration: The states that ruled in Marx's name industrialised quickly in places, but they were one-party dictatorships, and the famines and repression under Stalin and Mao alone cost tens of millions of lives. Most of these regimes collapsed between 1989 and 1991, though communist parties, or parties that grew out of them, still rule China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea. Historians still debate how much of this follows from Marx's ideas and how much from the choices of Lenin, Stalin, Mao and others.

scenes.title: Why Marx is still read
scenes.narration: Most economists reject much of Marx's economic theory, yet the questions he raised about inequality, crises and the power of capital are still at the centre of political argument, and interest in his work revived after the financial crisis of 2008. To see his answers set beside those of Adam Smith, Keynes and the free-market schools, PRP's Learning course reads a single recession six ways.

quiz.q: Where did Marx spend most of his adult life?
quiz.explain: He settled in London in 1849, after the defeat of the 1848 revolutions, and lived there until his death in 1883.

quiz.q: What did Marx call the value workers produce beyond what they are paid?
quiz.explain: In Capital, surplus value is the source of profit: the part of what workers produce for which they are not paid.

quiz.q: According to Robert Allen, what happened in Britain between 1780 and 1840?
options: Real wages rose faster than output
Output per worker rose by about 46 per cent, real wages by about 12
quiz.explain: Allen calls this Engels' pause. By his estimates the pattern reversed after 1840, when wages rose faster than output; other historians, such as Nicholas Crafts, find a smaller gap before 1840.

quiz.q: Who edited the second and third volumes of Capital?
quiz.explain: Engels prepared them from Marx's manuscripts; they appeared in 1885 and 1894.
